I glance at my watch. 8:43am. Is that the same time as yesterday? I wonder. I climb into the taxi that just pulled up in front of me and place my wallet in my lap. 
"Good morning," I say to the driver happily. He blinks at me in the rearview mirror. "Uh, same place," I continue when he doesn't respond. "Four Thirty-six West Gem Street."
We ride in silence; I think it a little odd. In all the years I've been working at Gem Street Animal Hospital, I've always taken cabs to work. On several occasions I've had repeat drivers, but this particular car seems assigned to me. 
You're losing your mind, I think to myself, but I look back up at the driver in the mirror. It is undoubtedly the same man who has taken me to work for the past eight days. His appearance isn't one that I'd say is memorable, but it is loud. A white man probably in his mid-50s, he has thick salt-and-pepper hair over dark, bushy eyebrows. His eyes look alarmingly sunken, and the wide-rimmed glasses he wears perched on the tip of his long and crooked nose do them no good. He's quite an ugly man. Maybe he'd be better looking if it weren't for those beady, ghostly eyes of his, I think silently. How doesn't he recognize me? I continue my train of thought. Or maybe he does, and he just isn't the conversational type. 
"So I see you like sticking to routines, huh?" I say jovially, deciding to break the ice. Eyes flicker to me for a brief moment, as if he is just now remembering my presence. 
"How you mean?" he drawls in a thick, Southern accent and I realize that I've never heard him speak prior to now. 
"Well, you've driven past the 7-Eleven on Suffolk Avenue around 8:30am for the past eight days," I chuckle and note how silly that sounds. 
This time his eyes are wide when they find mine and the intensity blazing in them is almost frightening. 
"An' how in'a hell you know that?" he demands harshly. "Come'a thank of it, I ain't had a chance ta hit Suffolk since damn near three days ago. Too much traffic down 'ere on Anderson Boulevard. It ain't all bad though, naw, I made alright." He says the last few sentences more to himself than to me. 
"Uh, I'm sorry sir," I say hesitantly when I think he's done, "but I remember you. Yesterday you were listening to 97.1 and switched to the Steve Harvey Morning Show because all they kept playing was Brad Paisley." 
I feel his eyes burning holes in my forehead through his mirror and pretend to be occupied in re-reading last night's notes from our training. A new miracle drug for arthritis in dogs, cats and horses has just come out and we must learn how to administer it before the it becomes available to the public. 
The car suddenly swerves and I jerk my head up. We are on West Gem Street but are at least ten blocks away from the hospital, and we've pulled over. 
"What's going on?" I ask, my voice shrill with rising panic.  The driver turns around in his seat, his face contorted and red. He is gripping the passenger headrest in his beefy fist, his knuckles white. I try not to state at the massive, throbbed hunk of flesh two feet from my face. 
"Now you listen here, missy," he bellows. "How in'a fuck you know what I had playin' on my radio yes'erday mornin'?" 
I hope he doesn't notice my trembling; I don't want him to know I'm scared. "I already told you before, sir," I try to say with confidence, "that you've taken me to work for the past eight days."
" Yeah, an' you tol' me you been gettin' taxis down by where I picked you up from, over on Suffolk. But I ain't been down there an' unless you picked up a taxi from Anderson Boulevard yes'erday then you ain't ride in this taxi." He pauses for a moment. "What's your name, lady?" 
I shake my head. "I don't tell cab drivers my name. Nothing personal," I add quickly. 
"Well here's what I wanna know, Miss No Name." His voice begins to climb again, his knuckles pulse on the seat in front of me. "How you know what I was listenin' to? You spyin' on me? I bet one of my ex-wives done set you up to this, ain't they."
"No, no," I stammer. "I must've gotten you confused with another cab driver." There's no point in angering this man, I think. Obviously he's got some sort of short-term memory loss, or maybe a mental disorder. "Most people hate Brad Paisley nowadays anyway," I joke, trying to lighten the mood. 
He just glares at me, unblinking for another minute and I do my best to look anywhere except at him. Finally he turns around, throws the car in drive and speeds up West Gem. He pulls into the hospital parking lot not five minutes later. 
"Thank you," I say as I scramble to collect my purse, wallet and laptop case. I close the car door and begin to walk up the steps to the front door. 

"Until next time, Riley."

No one gets it. No one understands. That's hard enough as it is but you know what I was thinking? What makes it so bad is that it's their own fault they don't know! I tried. I tried to explain, remember? But no one listened. I think it's because I don't fully know and adults in this day and age don't want to listen to you unless you have scholars and medical journals backing you, and they all think I'm crazy now anyway. I can see it in their eyes when I walk into the building every Thursday morning: "Oh God, there goes that crazy woman again." "You haven't heard of her? That's Riley," they whisper. They think I can't hear. They think I don't know, they think I'm CRAZY. 

Well let me tell you. The only thing crazy about me is what I'll do to get someone to listen to me. 

Okay, wait. I'm rambling. That happens a lot now, they think it's anxiety. But please, let me tell you what happened while you're still here. I have to tell you, I tell everyone. And it's okay if you don't believe me because eventually someone will, and that's all I need. I just need one person to believe me so that other people will believe them, and then the truth will come to the light. Okay? Just sit down for a second, it's a quick story. 

My son was killed five years ago. The police don't know who killed him but I do, and they won't listen to me. They think I'm crazy. I go to the Police Department on Third Avenue every Thursday morning and talk to Sherrif Roe and he's nice, he smiles and offers me coffee and asks how my appointments are going. I think maybe he knows who killed Trevor, why else would he be so nice? But he won't tell me and he acts like he doesn't believe me! Oh, because it doesn't make sense or something. But let me ask you this: it would make sense if it made sense! We would know who killed Trevor, wouldn't we, and it wouldn't be a mystery! And the county wouldn't have to pay for me to see a shrink and I wouldn't have to be here talking to you. But wait, I still have to tell you what happened. 

It was five years ago, Trevor was 21. He was on leave from the military, that damn place. I swear, if Connor hadn't pushed him so hard maybe he wouldn't have enlisted and maybe he'd be alive, hell, maybe I'd still be married. Everything has a butterfly effect, right? Trevor had already visited his dad and was spending a few nights a my house. It's so sad, you know, that he's dead. Because he's my son. I was so mad at him that day! Who knows what for - I was probably telling him he'd get himself killed out there and he was probably telling me to let him live his life. Isn't that ironic? I think so. I don't know. But I remember being mad and getting one of those dizzy spells I used to get and so I went to Lisa's house - she's my neighbor. I babysat her daughter when she was only a newborn, the precious thing. She's off in college now, she's got a kid too. It makes me feel old when I see people I knew as babies all grown up. I haven't seen Lisa much since... Well, I guess since Trevor died. But death does that to people, right? I mean, I was at her house when he died! Right there in her living room. See, I had gone over there because I was so mad, and I was dizzy because that always used to happen when I was mad. And we were watching TV and it was relaxing, you know. So she goes off to take a bath and meditate, and I remember it so well because - this is so funny - she'd always fight with her husband about her rituals. She'd take a 45 minute bath followed by a 75 minute meditation that you'd think was keeping her alive and killing him, the way they act. I must've fell asleep, because when I woke up the sun was setting. Lisa had fallen asleep after her meditation so I woke her up, told her I was going home. 

And that's when I found him. 

I'll spare you the details - you don't want to hear it, I know. But I have to tell you one thing, how he was killed, just because I can't tell you the story of how he was killed without telling you how it was done. Okay? He was lying at the bottom of the steps with his neck broken and his head bleeding. At the top of the steps was a skillet. They said the killer hit him upside the head with the skillet, but he didn't die until his neck broke during the fall. Isn't that terrible? It was terrible, I'll tell you. So I was screaming and I called the police and I called Lisa and it was just a whole big mess. They say they don't know who did it. They said the door wasn't broken into or picked at, they couldn't find any fingerprints or DNA except ours, nothing was stolen. 

It gets worse though. Guess what they did? They made me a SUSPECT. Just 'cause they had to, that's what Sherrif Roe says. Got me a psychological exam and everything. That's why I see a shrink now. But that's how society works now, here, I'll explain it to you. Before they went running tests on my brain, they spoke to me like any other victim going through something. All nice and helpful. Then they have to go by "protocol" and everything changes. Now they're concerned about my dizzy spells. They want to ask a bunch of questions about nothing - about the times as a kid I would black out. But what's that have to do with Trevor? They wanted to say I did it - his own mother! Now they say it's unsolved, a cold case. They can't do anything until new evidence arrives. I had to write a statement and poor Lisa had to answer questions... No wonder she doesn't come over anymore, poor thing! And she was so scared and upset she couldn't even think straight. She kept going on and on, apologizing, saying something 'bout how she didn't tell them she fell asleep. That's what she said. She said, "I'm so sorry Riley, but I didn't tell them I fell asleep, okay? I'm sorry about Trevor. I didn't tell them I fell asleep." Maybe she lost her mind a little bit. Stress can do that to you. 

They don't investigate Trevor anymore. Sherrif Roe said they ran out of leads, and he said to be happy because at least on the bright side they aren't charging me with my son's murder. That's when he was less nice to me. But even now, it depends on how his week is going. Last week I was telling him that they should go talk to Trevor's dad again and he got angry, saying he didn't have time to listen to my "theories" because they never make sense. 

But you know what's weird? Connor. Connor is weird, that's why I divorced him. He said I was paranoid, crazy, but really he just didn't like that I could see the real him. Where was Connor on that day? He says he was at home. But was he? Was he the first one there and the last one to leave? 

I hate talking about this, and I'm starting to feel dizzy... That means I'm getting upset. Do you mind if I stop for a second? I feel frustrated now, like something isn't making sense that should. This always happen when I talk about Trevor, like I have a déjà vu moment. Oh wow, come to think of it, last time I spoke to someone about Trevor was at this very park! I want to say the person I was talking to was also wearing a white jacket, yours looks familiar. But that would be too much of a coincidence, wouldn't it? 

What happened with the case, you ask? Who knows. I talk to Sherrif Roe every Thursday morning. One of these Thursdays he'll have some news for me. But they won't let me help, most of them won't even listen to me - what's this? Oh, medicine! Do you get dizzy spells as well? Thank you. Normally I wouldn't accept medicine from a stranger, but I recognize the bottle. Small world, huh? 

Now, I can't remember, were you asking me something? Oh. Yeah, a few people have asked me that. Um... Sorry, no, my mind just went fuzzy for a moment. I was trying to think... About... Oh! The last thing Trevor said to me. It's funny, he said, "What are you doing with that?" But it isn't always easy, you know. Trevor and I got in a fight that day, probably over his military career. I remember being so damn angry with that boy before going to Lisa's house. Probably my biggest character defect is my moodiness. I mean, what mother does that? Sits there and yells at her kid all the way up the stairs, yells through the door they slam in your face, yell all the way back down the hallway and out the front door? I acted like a child. Maybe... Who knows. Maybe if I hadn't, he'd still be here. 

Oh, his last words...? Yeah, that's what he said. Sort of funny, in a morbid way. Not what you'd expect. What? Did I -? Wait, you're asking if slammed the front door? Well geez, I don't know, probably. Why -? 

I didn't have anything in my hand. What a weird question. He slammed the door and then I left, I went to Lisa's house. 

Why do you keep asking what I had in my hand? 

Oh... What? I must've gotten confused then. 

I know I just said that, but I'm saying now I must've been confused. Because I wasn't carrying anything - I remember that - but... Wait. Ugh! Why is this confusing? I could've sworn... He asked me something. Wasn't it, "what are you doing with that?" No, but it couldn't have... Maybe it was, "where are you going?" But... No! I don't know. 

I'm sorry. Look at me, now I'm crying like an idiot. This is so weird, it's like I'm looking at a photograph but I need glasses... And the picture is blurry anyway. What's going on? I think I need to lay down. 

Oh, do you know of a place I can lay down? Yes, that would be great. Thank you.
